q: how to survive in the wilderness
wilderness survival basics
what to do if lost in the woods
survival priorities in the wild
a: When lost or stranded, remember the survival priorities in order — the 'rule of threes': you can survive ~3 minutes without air, ~3 hours without shelter from extreme cold/heat, ~3 days without water, ~3 weeks without food. So: (1) Stop and think — as soon as you realize you're lost, STOP (Stop, Think, Observe, Plan). Panic kills more people than the wilderness does; sit down, breathe, and assess. (2) Shelter first: in cold, wet, or windy conditions, shelter beats everything — get out of the wind, off the cold ground, and stay dry. A lean-to, a debris hut, or even a windbreak of branches can save your life. (3) Signal: three of anything (three whistle blasts, three fires, three rocks) is the universal distress signal; make yourself visible from the air (bright clothing, a large ground signal). Stay put if you've told someone where you're going — searchers find stationary people. (4) Water: find a stream and boil or purify it (boiling 1 minute is the most reliable); don't drink stagnant water without treating it. (5) Fire: dry wood, a fire bow, or a lighter if you carry one — fire gives warmth, signaling, and boiled water. (6) Food last — you can go weeks without it, and foraging mistakes can kill you faster than hunger. The biggest survival asset is preparation: tell someone your route, carry the ten essentials (navigation, headlamp, sun protection, insulation, fire, repair kit, first aid, knife, shelter, water/food). Most 'survival' situations are really 'wait for rescue comfortably' situations — the people who die are usually the ones who wandered deeper in panic.

q: how to start a fire without matches
how to start a fire with sticks
how to make a fire bow
how to start a fire in the wilderness
a: The classic methods, in order of practicality: (1) Ferro rod (a fire starter you carry) — scrape it with a knife edge and it throws hot sparks; it works wet and is the most reliable non-match option. (2) Battery + steel wool — touch a 9V battery (or any battery) to fine steel wool; it glows and you blow it into flame (the steel wool carries the current). (3) Magnifying glass or glasses lens — focus sunlight on char cloth, dry tinder, or even a black mark on paper. (4) The bow drill — the classic friction method: a bow (curved branch + shoelace), a spindle (dry, straight stick), a fireboard, and a handhold; spin the spindle against the board with the bow until you produce a glowing ember, then transfer it to your tinder bundle (dry grass, bark, cotton) and blow gently. It works, but it takes practice and dry wood — expect to burn through attempts. The universal keys: (1) Preparation is everything — have a bird's nest of fine, dry tinder ready BEFORE you start sparking; a good ember dies in seconds without tinder. (2) Dry materials — wet wood won't ignite; split logs to find dry heartwood and shave it fine. (3) Build the fire structure (teepee or log cabin with airflow) before lighting. Practice the bow drill at home once, and carry a ferro rod — the combination covers 99% of real scenarios.

q: how to find clean water in the wild
how to purify water in the wild
how to find water in the wilderness
how to make wild water safe to drink
a: Finding water: look for moving water (streams, rivers) — moving beats stagnant; animal tracks often lead to water; morning dew on grass can be wiped up with a cloth and wrung into a container; and in a survival situation, a still (dig a hole, cover with a sheet, place a cup in the center under the drip point) can distill moisture from soil and vegetation. But finding it is only half — purification is the part that prevents dysentery, giardia, and worse. In order of reliability: (1) Boiling — the gold standard: bring it to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute (3 minutes above 2,000 m / 6,500 ft elevation). This kills pathogens — it doesn't remove chemical contamination, but it makes water safe from the biology that will actually make you sick. (2) Filtration — a filter (Sawyer, LifeStraw, or any water filter with 0.2-micron pores) removes protozoa and bacteria on the spot; pair with chemical treatment for viruses. (3) Chemical treatment — iodine tablets or chlorine dioxide drops kill most pathogens but take 30 minutes to hours and don't remove sediment or taste great. The myth to avoid: clear water is not clean water — mountain streams are the classic source of giardia; 'it looks fine' is not treatment. The other myth: snow can be eaten straight (it lowers your core temperature and wastes energy) — melt it and boil it. When in doubt: filter, then boil.

q: how to treat hypothermia
hypothermia first aid
what to do for hypothermia
signs of hypothermia
a: Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C (95°F) — it kills by shutting the body down, and it's the classic silent killer of outdoor accidents (it can happen in 10°C weather, especially wet and windy). Recognize it: shivering (early), then confusion, clumsiness, slurred speech, and shivering stopping (late — a bad sign). Treatment: (1) Get them out of the cold and wet — into shelter, dry clothes, and a sleeping bag or blankets. Handle gently — rough handling of a severely hypothermic person can trigger cardiac arrest. (2) Warm the core first: warm (not hot) drinks if they're alert and can swallow, warm compresses on chest/neck/groin, and body heat (skin-to-skin inside a sleeping bag). Do NOT warm the arms and legs first — warming extremities pushes cold blood to the core and can cause 'after-drop', a lethal temperature drop. (3) Do not rub or massage limbs, no alcohol (dilates blood vessels and accelerates heat loss), and no hot water bottles directly on skin (burn risk without sensation). (4) Severe cases — unconscious, barely breathing, no shivering — are medical emergencies: call for help, keep them stable, and handle as gently as possible; rewarming must happen carefully, ideally in a medical setting. The prevention side matters most: cotton kills (it holds water against skin — wool or synthetics instead), and wet + wind is the dangerous combo; always carry a dry layer and emergency shelter on outdoor trips.

q: how to treat a snake bite
snake bite first aid
what to do if bitten by a snake
how to treat a venomous snake bite
a: First, the updates: modern guidance has changed a lot. DO: (1) Move away from the snake calmly — a second bite is a real risk. (2) Keep the victim calm and still, with the bitten limb immobilized below heart level if possible — movement pumps venom into circulation faster. (3) Remove rings, watches, and tight clothing near the bite before swelling starts. (4) Get to a hospital as fast as possible — antivenom is the only real treatment for venomous bites; call ahead so they can prepare. (5) Note the snake's appearance (color, pattern, head shape) from a safe distance — a photo helps doctors choose antivenom, but never risk a second bite to get it. DO NOT: (1) Cut the wound and suck out venom — it doesn't work, damages tissue, and puts venom in your mouth. (2) Apply a tourniquet (except for some Australian elapid bites, where a firm pressure-immobilization bandage is recommended — check local guidance). (3) Apply ice, heat, or electric shock — all myths that worsen tissue damage. (4) Drink alcohol or caffeine. (5) Chase or kill the snake — that's how most bites to the rescuer happen. Reassurance matters: most snake bites are 'dry' (no venom injected, up to 50% for some species), but you can't tell — treat every bite as venomous and get medical care. Keep the victim warm, calm, and as still as possible during transport.
